1.1.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "classify hip arthroplasty"
- "**Arthroplasty** = reconstructive joint surgery → resection, interposition or replacement."
- "Replacement → **hemiarthroplasty** (unipolar, bipolar) or **total hip arthroplasty (THA)**."
- "THA → **stem, head, liner, cup** · instability → **tripolar / dual mobility**."

### Definition & resection arthroplasty
- **Arthroplasty** = reconstructive joint surgery → a prosthesis is not always needed
- No prosthesis → **interposition** or **partial resection** of the native joint
- Define it broadly → resection stays an option, e.g. after a failed infected implant
- **Resection arthroplasty** → head ± neck, proximal femur and/or acetabulum removed

#### Girdlestone & interposition
- Classic → **Girdlestone** (head + neck) → salvage for uncontrollable periprosthetic infection
- 1800s → resection for **tuberculosis** · **Girdlestone 1928** → wide excision · 1943 → pyogenic hips (Surgery of the Hip)
- Interposition survives in small joints → trapeziectomy + **LRTI** (ligament reconstruction, tendon interposition)

### Hemiarthroplasty vs THA
- **Hemiarthroplasty** = femoral head only · **THA** = head + acetabulum
- Hemi needs healthy acetabular cartilage → metal rubs on it → never for an arthritic hip
- Failure → **acetabular erosion**, protrusio, groin pain → often conversion to THA

#### Choosing in a displaced neck fracture
| Surgery of the Hip | **THA** | **Hemiarthroplasty** |
|---|---|---|
| Patient | lucid, independent community walker | low demand, minimal walker |
| Mind · life expectancy | intact · >5 years | impaired · short |
| Outcome | better function, fewer reoperations | erosion, worse pain scores if active |

- **Baker RCT** (n=81), 3 years → THA: fewer complications, longer walks, higher **Oxford Hip Score**
[[FIG: Fig 1.1 · 1.1
- Same trial → hemi: **>60%** acetabular erosion on X-ray
- **Bipolar** → safe at 75 · at 60–70 may fail by 10–15 years (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 1.2 · 1.1
- Never bipolar in the young · short life but acetabular pain → total, by **physiological** age

#### Other femoral-side replacements
- Metastasis in head or neck → **cemented** hemi: chemo- and radiotherapy spoil ingrowth
[[FIG: Fig 1.3 · 1.1
- **Hemi-resurfacing** (metal-on-cartilage) → flattened head, acetabulum spared → temporising only

### Unipolar hemiarthroplasty — Austin Moore vs Thompson
- **Unipolar** = one-piece monoblock → moves only on the native acetabulum · head size fixed

| | **Austin Moore** | **Thompson** |
|---|---|---|
| Stem | **fenestrated** (windows) | **solid**, collared |
| Fixation | uncemented → bone grows through windows | **cemented** |
| X-ray | windows, no cement mantle | cement mantle |
| Neck | cut → seated on the calcar | cut → seated on the calcar |

- Both need a neck cut → "Austin Moore without osteotomy" is wrong (Rockwood)
[[FIG: Fig 1.4 · 1.1
- Loose Austin Moore → **subsides** and toggles → thigh pain
- Wrong head size → focal contact stress → **cartilage erosion**
- Cemented → poor bone, low demand · uncemented → good bone, younger, higher demand

### Bipolar hemiarthroplasty
- **Bipolar** = two bearings → inner head in a PE-lined shell · shell on the acetabulum
- Wider safe **ROM** (range of motion) → impingement later → more stable
- Theory → less cartilage motion · reality → inner bearing often stops → acts unipolar
- **Modular** → head size, neck length (short, standard, long), cemented or cementless

#### Where it falls short
- Inner PE (polyethylene) = extra **wear** source a unipolar lacks
[[FIG: Fig 1.5 · 1.1
- Rare **dissociation** of shell from inner head → usually at closed reduction

PITFALL — is bipolar better than unipolar?
- Theory → two bearings spare the cartilage · trials → no better function or durability
- Say → "**no proven benefit; unipolar is more cost-effective** (Surgery of the Hip)"

#### Bipolar as salvage for instability
- Recurrent THA dislocation → remove cup → bipolar head on remaining acetabular bone
- Two bearings → larger safe arc · larger head → bigger **jump distance**
- **Parvizi & Morrey** → dislocation prevented in **81%** of 27 hips at 5 years

#### Its price
- Risk → **migration** from acetabular erosion · groin pain not rare

### Standard THA components
- **Stem, head, liner, cup** → one bearing: head ↔ liner → wear and most dislocations start there
- Head + liner modular → **exchanged** at revision if stem and cup are well fixed
- Indications → **PE wear** or acute infection: DAIR (debridement, antibiotics, implant retention)
- Modular junctions add failure sites → **trunnionosis** = fretting-crevice corrosion at the head–neck taper

#### Modular versus monoblock cups
- Trunnionosis → metal ions even with metal-on-PE · favoured by large heads, mixed metals
- **Modular PE liners** (1980s) → stability options in theatre + later bearing exchange
[[FIG: Fig 1.6 · 1.1
- **Offset liner** (7 mm) → more stable, but cup loosening **4.0% vs 0.12%** (Surgery of the Hip)
- **Morscher cup** = monoblock → PE moulded into a titanium mesh shell → no screws

#### The cementless cup (Prof Fady Kamal)
- Monoblock → no backside wear, no screws → obsolete · shell + liner → exchangeable
[[FIG: Fig 1.7 · 1.1
- Material → cobalt-chrome, titanium or tantalum · now mostly **titanium**: porous, lower modulus, press-fit
- **Tantalum** → more porous, expensive
- Shapes (1983) → cylindrical, square, conical, ellipsoid · now only **hemispherical**
[[FIG: Fig 1.8 · 1.1

| Generation | Design | Problem or gain |
|---|---|---|
| 1st · World War II era | stainless steel + screws | mechanical fixation only |
| 2nd · early 1980s | **vertical** cups | edge loading, locking failures |
| 3rd · 2000s | hemi-ellipsoid, PE irradiated without air, trimmed rim, polished inside | less **backside wear**, dissociation, impingement |

- Third generation → rim trimmed so the neck does not impinge
[[FIG: Fig 1.9 · 1.1
- **Dual radius** → obsolete: can fracture the acetabulum · single radius obsolete too
[[FIG: Fig 1.10 · 1.1
- **Hemi-ellipsoid** → rim 2 mm wider than the dome → peripheral press-fit
- Liners → **neutral** · **lipped** 10° or 20°
[[FIG: Fig 1.11 · 1.1

#### Liner options
- **Offset** ± lip → restores offset and leg length · **captive** → a ring constrains the head
[[FIG: Fig 1.12 · 1.1

### Tripolar & dual mobility
- Indication → **recurrent dislocation** · also high-risk primaries
- **Tripolar** → 3 interfaces: inner head → bipolar head → PE liner, in a shell
- **Dual mobility** → small head in a large PE liner, which moves in a polished cup
[[FIG: Fig 1.13 · 1.1
- Liner = a big head → higher **head-to-neck ratio** → wider arc, bigger jump distance

#### Not a bipolar
- Dual mobility → large cup fixed in the acetabulum = a **total hip** · tripolar = dual mobility
[[FIG: Fig 1.14 · 1.1

#### When it is used
- **Unconstrained tripolar** = bipolar head in shell + liner → succeeds in revision for instability
[[FIG: Fig 1.15 · 1.1
- Tripolar → well-fixed nonmodular stem with no large-head option
- Complex acetabular rebuild → tripolar spares the cup a constrained liner's shear
- Primary **dual mobility** → spine pathology, elderly neck fracture (Campbell) · neuromuscular, weak abductors

#### Cases & results
- Failed ceramic-on-ceramic in a young patient → revised to dual mobility
[[FIG: Fig 1.16 · 1.1
- Cognitively impaired → tripolar / dual mobility for stability
[[FIG: Fig 1.17 · 1.1
- Tripolar results very good · Egypt → one cemented dual mobility, one company
- **Constrained tripolar** → 0 dislocations in 110 revisions at 3.2 years · cup lucencies 14%
[[FIG: Fig 1.18 · 1.1

#### Failure modes
- **Su & Pellici** → 97.6% of 85 hips stable at 4.8 years (Surgery of the Hip)
- Tripolar failures → bone–implant interface · liner–shell lock · bipolar lock · inner-bearing dislocation
- Unique to dual mobility → **intraprosthetic dislocation**: small head escapes a worn liner rim
- X-ray sign → head **eccentric** inside the cup

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Hemi needs cartilage · Moore windows, Thompson cement · bipolar unproven · dual mobility = big head**

1.2.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which material goes where?"
- "**Stem** → metal with fatigue strength · **head** → always hard: cobalt-chrome or ceramic."
- "**Liner** → soft PE or hard → hard-on-soft or hard-on-hard bearing."
- "Commonest now → metal or ceramic on **HXLPE** (highly cross-linked PE) · stiff stems → **stress shielding**."

### Where each material goes
- **Stem** → always metal, primary fixation · millions of cycles → high **fatigue strength**
- Stems → α+β or β **titanium alloys** · cups → **titanium** shells
- **Head** → hard only → its whole surface is always loaded, each liner point part-time
- **Liner** → hard or soft → the soft partner always sits on the liner side

#### The bearing
- **Friction interface** = head–liner · bearing system → liner + head + fluid + soft tissue
[[FIG: Fig 1.19 · 1.2
- Standard bearing in the USA → metal head on **UHMWPE** (ultra-high-molecular-weight PE)
- Bigger head in the same cup → thinner PE → avoid conventional PE **<6 mm**
- Failed **locking mechanism** → liner rotates or dissociates: squeak, clunk, apparent dislocation

#### Material terms (Prof Fahmy)
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Biomaterial** | any substance used to treat, augment or replace tissue, organ or function |
| **Brittle** vs **ductile** | little plastic deformation (glass, ceramic) vs much (stainless steel) |
| **Notch sensitivity** | fracture from a crack or scratch → high in brittle materials |
| **Hardness** | resists scratching and indentation → highest in **ceramic** |

- **Young's modulus** = elastic slope → ceramic > metal alloys > cortical bone > cement > PE
[[FIG: Fig 1.20 · 1.2
- **Toughness** = area under the curve = energy absorbed → more precise than UTS
[[FIG: Fig 1.21 · 1.2
- UTS = ultimate tensile strength · hip load → **3×** body weight walking, ≈**5×** stairs, jogging
[[FIG: Fig 1.22 · 1.2

### Bearing couples
- **Hard-on-soft** → forgiving, but PE debris · **hard-on-hard** → less wear
- Hard-on-hard costs → ceramic is brittle, metal releases ions · allows large heads → stability
- **Ceramic-on-PE** → avoids brittleness, fewer ions than **MoM** (metal-on-metal)
- Historic order → cobalt-chrome on UHMWPE, then MoM, then alumina-on-alumina

#### Hard-on-hard problems
- **High-carbon** cobalt-chrome (>0.2%) → hard carbides, scratch resistant · low-carbon → softer, more wear
- MoM cobalt and chromium **ions** → alternatives sought → **ceramic-on-metal** (2001)
- Ceramic-on-metal → less metal wear than MoM in the simulator
- **Squeaking** → specific to **CoC** (ceramic-on-ceramic) → edge loading from malposition

#### Choosing the couple — two schools
| Age (Prof Fawzy) | Couple |
|---|---|
| <60, active | CoC, large head 32–36 mm |
| 65–75 | ceramic on cross-linked PE |
| >75 | cobalt-chrome on cross-linked PE |

- Choice → **sensible, not absolute**: evidence, benefit–risk, price, age, activity, comorbidity, life expectancy
- CoC with care → **ligamentous laxity**, large preoperative ROM, deformity
- Other school → no CoC · metal-on-PE ≈**30-year** registry survival (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Same school → a 39-year-old gets hard-on-soft: metal or ceramic on PE

PITFALL — CoC or hard-on-soft for the young?
- Prof Fawzy → CoC under 60 · Prof Sherif Khaled → hard-on-soft even at 39
- Say → "**both are accepted; hard-on-soft is forgiving, CoC needs exact cup position**"

- **Alumina-on-alumina** for the young → 328 hips, mean 54: equal to metal-on-PE at 5 years

### Metals & stress shielding
- **Alloy** = metal + other elements → stronger, harder, corrosion resistant

| Metal (Prof Fahmy) | Strength | Weakness | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stainless steel** | very stiff | stress shielding, corrosion | cemented stems |
| **Cobalt-chromium** | corrosion resistant, low wear, highest modulus | stress shielding | **heads**, cemented stems |
| **Titanium** | biocompatible, low modulus | poor wear | uncemented stems, cups |
| **Tantalum** | low modulus, very porous | expensive | acetabular reconstruction |

- Head → **cobalt-chrome**: stiff, least toxic, bioinert · stainless steel not bioinert enough
[[FIG: Fig 1.23 · 1.2
- Titanium off bearings → it **scratches and wears**, not "too flexible" (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 1.24 · 1.2
- **316L** steel for decades → Rex 734, Ortron-90 stronger · nickel allergy → BioDur 108
- BioDur 108 → fracture fixation only · titanium vs cobalt-chrome → denser bone, more ingrowth
[[FIG: Fig 1.25 · 1.2

#### Corrosion — metals only
- All materials fail by **wear** and **fatigue** · metals also by **corrosion**
[[FIG: Fig 1.26 · 1.2
- **Galvanic** → two different metals, e.g. stainless steel + cobalt-chrome → never mix
- **Crevice** → in cracks or scratches → stainless steel most prone
- **Fretting** → micromotion → always at the head–neck junction

#### How stress shielding arises
- Stiff stem takes the load → proximal femur unloaded → resorption = **Wolff's law** reversed
[[FIG: Fig 1.27 · 1.2
- Mismatch → high stress at the **distal tip** (fracture) · low elsewhere → disuse atrophy
- Stiff cobalt-chrome stem → thigh pain · fully porous stem → load goes to the diaphysis
- Incidence → **23%** fully porous stems · **18%** AML (anatomic medullary locking)
[[FIG: Fig 1.28 · 1.2

| Factor | Higher risk |
|---|---|
| Material | cobalt-chrome > titanium |
| Coating | extensive > proximal · rigid fixation |
| Design | solid > hollow |
| Diameter | larger → +20% ≈ 2× stiffness (radius⁴) |
| Bone | preoperative osteopenia |

#### Reducing it
- Modulus → titanium 110 vs cobalt-chrome 220 GPa → little clinical difference (Surgery of the Hip)
- **Proximal-only porous coating** → less shielding, fixation intact
[[FIG: Fig 1.29 · 1.2
- **Tapered titanium stem** → osseointegrated by ≈12 weeks → graded load, less thigh pain
- **Epoch** composite (cobalt-chrome core, PAEK, titanium mesh) → less bone loss over 7 years

#### Does it matter?
- **Calcar rounding**, thinning in **Gruen zones 1 and 7**, stem fixed → not loosening
[[FIG: Fig 1.30 · 1.2
- At 14 years → bone loss without more revision, osteolysis or thigh pain
- Matters at **revision** → too little bone for a standard proximal-fit stem

### Ceramics — alumina vs zirconia
- Bearing ceramics → **alumina**, **zirconia** · in use → alumina, m-ZR, **AMC** (alumina matrix composite)
- **CoC** = alumina-on-alumina → zirconia wears badly against itself
- Strong in compression, weak in bending → **hard, brittle** · head and liner only
[[FIG: Fig 1.31 · 1.2
- Cannot mould round a mismatched head · alumina **ISO 6474** since 1984 → most inert

| Ceramic (Prof Fahmy) | Wear | Fracture risk |
|---|---|---|
| Alumina | very low | brittle |
| Zirconia | higher | lower |
| **AMC** (BIOLOX delta) | minimal | very low |

- AMC → alumina = surface, zirconia = strength → ≈50–60% tougher than alumina
- Generations 1974 → **2003 BIOLOX delta** → smaller grains, far fewer fractures
[[FIG: Fig 1.32 · 1.2
- **Oxidized zirconium** → metal alloy with a ceramic surface, not solid ceramic
- **Hydrophilic** → wettable, low friction · contact angle metal 86°, ceramic 45°
[[FIG: Fig 1.33 · 1.2

#### Why pure zirconia went
- Phase change in body fluid → weaker, rougher, more wear → hence composites
- **Yttria-stabilised** → tetragonal → monoclinic: grains expand 4%
- One maker's process change → ball fractures, recall → ended 2001 · m-ZR still used

#### Fracture
- **Boutin** 1970 → large impure grains, frequent fracture · Morse taper 1977 → 2% · now 0.004%
- Short neck = 2× long-neck strength · 32 mm 60% stronger than 28 mm · abduction <50°
- Wright series → 1709 CoC hips at 8 years → catastrophic fracture **0.2%**
- Rare now → more with poor technique, e.g. cup **retroversion** · unforgiving, expensive

#### Revision after fracture (Prof Fawzy)
- **BIOLOX delta** pink → fracture often unseen on X-ray → pain, squeak → **CT** → revise soon
[[FIG: Fig 1.34 · 1.2
- Revise to a **ceramic head** → residual ceramic = third body → destroys a metal head
[[FIG: Fig 1.35 · 1.2
- Taper intact, stem stable → ceramic head with **metal sleeve** · taper damaged → revise stem
- Suction tool lifts the liner · check taper → "**Once a ceramic, always a ceramic**"
[[FIG: Fig 1.36 · 1.2

#### Pros & cons
- Pros → **less wear and osteolysis** · scratch resistant → less third-body wear
- **Squeaking** → usually low, >10% in some series · rim impingement, stripe wear (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 1.37 · 1.2
- Concerns → fracture, no lipped inserts, limited modularity, exact positioning, cost
[[FIG: Fig 1.38 · 1.2

### Comparison of bearing surfaces
| Criterion (Handbook) | Order |
|---|---|
| Price | metal-on-PE cheapest → CoC dearest |
| Head size | MoM largest, thinnest cup → stability, ROM |
| Wear | **metal-on-PE** highest → MoM → CoC lowest |
| Toxicity | CoC lowest (bioinert) → MoM highest |
| Modularity | common, cheap couples high · rare, dear ones low |

- MoM toxicity → renal failure, crosses the placenta, early pseudotumour, nickel urticaria
- No MoM → **renal impairment** or women who may conceive · ions are renally cleared

#### Wear and head size
- MoM → **40–100×** less wear than metal-on-PE, but nanometre particles (Surgery of the Hip)
[[FIG: Fig 1.39 · 1.2
- Hard-on-hard or **HXLPE** → very low osteolysis at 10 years
- MoM → larger head + low clearance → fluid film → less wear: opposite of metal-on-PE
- **Charnley** → PE wear ∝ sliding distance → small head, half the socket

| Couple (Prof Fahmy) | Linear wear, µm/year |
|---|---|
| Cobalt-chrome / PE | 120–200 |
| Ceramic / PE | 80–120 |
| Cobalt-chrome / HXLPE | 0–25 |
| MoM · ceramic / metal | 1–5 · 1 |
| CoC | <1 |

- Volumetric → CoC and MoM least, metal-on-PE most
[[FIG: Fig 1.40 · 1.2
- Large modular MoM → low wear, stable, less impingement: high head-to-neck ratio
[[FIG: Fig 1.41 · 1.2

#### Metal-on-metal safety
- Concerns → lymphocytic aggregates, **metal ions**, hypersensitivity · 35% of US hips in 2005
[[FIG: Fig 1.42 · 1.2
- Large-head modular → cobalt and chromium ↑↑ → junctions blamed · blood cobalt ↑5–10-fold
- **Run-in** → ions rise in year 1, then fall · a later rise = trouble (Prof Fawzy)
[[FIG: Fig 1.43 · 1.2
- **ALVAL** (aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesion) → pseudotumour → most MoM withdrawn
[[FIG: Fig 1.44 · 1.2

#### Reaction & work-up
- Reaction = **ALTR / ARMD** (adverse local tissue reaction / reaction to metal debris)
- Local → metallosis, pseudotumour, bone loss · systemic → ions, toxicity, carcinogenesis
- Painful MoM hip → serum **cobalt and chromium** + **MARS-MRI** (metal artefact reduction sequence)

#### Resurfacing, ceramic limits, polyethylene
- **Resurfacing** (MoM) → neck fracture, notching, technique-sensitive · no females: small necks

### Types & modes of wear
- **Wear** = material eroded by another surface · in the hip → **adhesive, abrasive, corrosive**
[[FIG: Fig 1.47 · 1.3

| Type | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Adhesive** | bonds weld the surfaces → spot welding at the trunnion → trunnionosis |
| **Abrasive** (two-body) | **ploughing** → asperities of the harder surface scratch PE |
| **Three-body** | debris, cement or bone wedged between the surfaces |
| **Fatigue** | repeated stress → microcracks coalesce → a piece breaks off |
| **Backside** | liner moving on its metal shell or tibial baseplate |
| **Stripe** | ceramic **edge loading** after microseparation → stripe on head and liner |

| McKellop mode (Surgery of the Hip) | What rubs |
|---|---|
| 1 · Regular sliding | the intended bearing surfaces |
| 2 · Impingement | bearing on non-bearing surface, e.g. head on cup edge |
| 3 · Three-body | a third body between the bearing surfaces |
| 4 · Backside (fretting) | two non-bearing surfaces, e.g. backside, taper |

- Types say **how** · modes say **which surfaces** rub
- Hip = **multidirectional sliding** → crossing tracks → more debris
[[FIG: Fig 1.48 · 1.3
- Abrasion = the third-body mechanism → cement particles, worn MoM **carbides**
[[FIG: Fig 1.49 · 1.3
- Cement or bone left at closure → third body → irrigate before reduction

### Polyethylene wear — physical factors
- PE = most wear-prone → the **weakest link**
[[FIG: Fig 1.62 · 1.3

- Protect it → trial reductions against retractors or cup edges scratch it
- Wear ∝ **sliding distance** → bigger head = more volumetric wear in conventional PE

#### Cup and activity
- Cup inclination **>50°**, malalignment, unrestored offset → more wear
- More debris in **active** patients, not heavy ones · aerobic fine · no running, heavy lifting

### Polyethylene — manufacture, sterilisation & shelf life
- **UHMWPE** → >200,000 monomers, linear homopolymer · cross-links → wear resistant
- **Direct compression moulding** → clinical wear half that of machined PE
- **Ram-bar extrusion** → calcium stearate impurities → more wear

| Sterilisation (Prof Fahmy) | Effect |
|---|---|
| Ethylene oxide, gas plasma | no cross-linking, properties unchanged → inferior wear |
| Gamma in air (cobalt-60, 2–4 Mrad) | radicals + oxygen → **oxidation** → weak PE |
| Gamma in vacuum or inert gas | radicals → **cross-links** → wear ↓ |

- Irradiation breaks a covalent bond → **free radical** → oxygen: degradation · none: cross-link
- Irradiation **creates** radicals, never removes them → heat or vitamin E does
[[FIG: Fig 1.63 · 1.3
- Gamma vs ethylene oxide → simulator wear ↓30–46% · inert packaging → ↓15–30%
- Gamma-in-air PE → subsurface **white band** of oxidation on retrieval

#### Cross-linking — gain and cost
- **HXLPE** → wear ↓40–95% → smaller particles (Surgery of the Hip)
[[FIG: Fig 1.65 · 1.3
- Larger head on HXLPE → no rise in volumetric wear
[[FIG: Fig 1.66 · 1.3
- 32, 36, 40 mm heads → HXLPE only · UHMWPE → late osteolysis (Prof Fady Kamal)
[[FIG: Fig 1.67 · 1.3
- Dose up to **8–10 Mrad** → more wear resistance, less fatigue and fracture strength

#### Weak rims
- Thin or unsupported HXLPE at the rim lock → **rim fracture**
[[FIG: Fig 1.68 · 1.3

| Heat (Prof Fahmy) | Radicals | Crystallinity | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Remelting** | all removed | falls (40%) | fatigue cracking |
| **Annealing** (below melting) | remain | kept (60%) | in-vivo oxidation |

- Vitamin E → stabilises radicals without remelting's strength loss
- Shelf life → radicals meet oxygen → oxidation → wear · visible after >4 years
- Oxidation → toughness and fatigue ↓↓ → catastrophic failure · irreversible → prevent it
